words.definition: Quick to feel and show anger over small provocations.
words.example: One more interruption and the irascible old cook hurled his ladle across the kitchen.
words.mnemonic: Sounds like 'ire' + 'rascal' — an ire-filled rascal ready to blow up at any moment.

words.definition: Having a calm temperament that is rarely stirred to strong emotion.
words.example: While the others panicked at the fire alarm, Tom stayed phlegmatic and finished his coffee.
words.mnemonic: From 'phlegm,' the sluggish body humor once believed to make people slow and unexcitable.

words.definition: Prone to sudden and unpredictable changes of mood or mind.
words.example: His mercurial temper meant a shared joke could curdle into fury before the punchline landed.
words.mnemonic: Named for Mercury — the fast-darting messenger god and quicksilver, which never stays put.

words.definition: Warm and easy to talk to; pleasant and approachable in manner.
words.example: The affable bartender remembered every regular's name and their usual order.
words.mnemonic: 'Affable' → 'have a ball' — you have a ball chatting with such an easy host.

words.definition: Having a friendly, pleasant, and good-natured disposition.
words.example: Their amiable neighbor waved every morning and always offered to water the plants.
words.mnemonic: From Latin 'amicus' (friend) — think French 'ami'; someone easy to befriend.

words.definition: Pleasant and agreeable because of shared tastes or a friendly nature.
words.example: We fell in with a congenial group of hikers who liked the same slow pace and long lunches.
words.mnemonic: 'Con-' (together) + 'genial' — people of the same kind sharing a warm spirit.

words.definition: Disliking and distrusting other people in general.
words.example: The misanthropic recluse posted 'Go Away' signs and hadn't opened his door in years.
words.mnemonic: Greek 'miso-' (hate) + 'anthropos' (human) — a hater of humankind.

words.definition: Sulky and irritable in a childish, unreasonable way.
words.example: Told to wait his turn, he gave a petulant huff and folded his arms like a toddler.
words.mnemonic: 'Petulant' → 'pet' + 'ant' — a spoiled pet ant throwing tiny tantrums.

words.definition: Bad-tempered, argumentative, and difficult to deal with.
words.example: The cantankerous landlord bickered about the rent, the paint, and the weather all at once.
words.mnemonic: Sounds like 'can't-anchor-us' — so quarrelsome no one can settle near him.

words.definition: Rude, unfriendly, and bad-tempered in manner.
words.example: The surly waiter slapped down the menus and walked off without a word.
words.mnemonic: 'Surly' → 'sir-ly' — a haughty 'sir' who is gruff and rude to everyone.

words.definition: Silently gloomy and bad-humored, showing quiet resentment.
words.example: The teenager sat sullen at dinner, glaring at his plate and refusing to speak.
words.mnemonic: 'Sullen' → 'sully' (to stain) — a darkened, stained mood; a sun that won't shine.

words.definition: Stern, gloomy, and unsmiling in appearance or manner.
words.example: The dour headmaster surveyed the assembly without a flicker of a smile.
words.mnemonic: 'Dour' rhymes with 'sour' — picture a sour, grim, humorless face.

words.definition: Having a gloomy, cold, and sardonic temperament.
words.example: His saturnine expression darkened the room before he had said a single word.
words.mnemonic: From the planet Saturn — those born under slow, gloomy Saturn were thought grim and melancholy.

words.definition: In very low spirits from loss of hope or courage; deeply dejected.
words.example: After the third rejection letter, she grew despondent and stopped submitting her work.
words.mnemonic: 'De-' (down) + 'spond' (spirit, as in respond) — the spirit sinking, no response of hope.

words.definition: Sad and lonely, especially from being abandoned or left behind.
words.example: A forlorn puppy shivered on the doorstep, watching the empty road for its owner.
words.mnemonic: 'Forlorn' → 'forsaken' + 'lorn' (lost) — utterly lost and left behind.

words.definition: Full of a quiet, yearning sadness for something loved but now gone.
words.example: She gazed at her childhood home with a wistful smile, remembering the summers spent there.
words.mnemonic: Sounds like 'wish' + 'full' — full of wishes for what you can no longer have.

words.definition: Cheerful, good-humored, and full of warm friendliness.
words.example: The jovial host greeted every guest with a hearty laugh and a slap on the back.
words.mnemonic: From Jove (Jupiter), the god whose planet was said to make people merry.

words.definition: Overflowing with lively energy, joy, and enthusiasm.
words.example: The children were exuberant on the last day of school, shouting and sprinting across the field.
words.mnemonic: 'Ex-YOU-berant' — energy bursting out of you like a shaken soda can.

words.definition: Attractively full of life, spirit, and animated charm.
words.example: Her vivacious personality lit up the party the moment she walked through the door.
words.mnemonic: Contains 'viva' (Latin for life) — a vivacious person is bursting with life.

words.definition: Calm, peaceful, and not easily disturbed or upset.
words.example: The placid lake mirrored the mountains without a single ripple.
words.mnemonic: Shares a root with 'placate' and 'please' — a placid surface is at peace.

words.definition: Showing little emotion and staying unmoved by excitement or distress.
words.example: The guard remained stolid even as the crowd screamed and pushed against the gate.
words.mnemonic: Sounds like 'solid' — a stolid person is emotionally solid and unshaken.

words.definition: Not revealing any feeling through the face or manner.
words.example: The judge listened with an impassive face, betraying no hint of her verdict.
words.mnemonic: 'Im-' (not) + 'passion' — no passion showing, just a blank mask.

words.definition: Shy and lacking belief in one's own abilities.
words.example: Too diffident to raise his hand, he kept the right answer to himself.
words.mnemonic: Line it up against 'confident' and swap the start — it is the opposite of confident.

words.definition: Nervous, easily frightened, and full of hesitant fear.
words.example: The timorous kitten fled under the couch at the slightest sound.
words.mnemonic: From Latin 'timor' (fear); think 'timid' — a timorous creature is timid and afraid.

words.definition: Weak-willed and cowardly, shrinking from anything difficult or risky.
words.example: His pusillanimous refusal to speak up let the bully win unchallenged.
words.mnemonic: Latin 'pusillus' (tiny) + 'animus' (spirit) — a spirit too tiny to be brave.

words.definition: Shamefully lacking courage; despicably fearful.
words.example: In a craven move, he abandoned his friends and ran at the first sign of danger.
words.mnemonic: Picture a 'raven' fleeing the nest — a craven soul craves nothing but escape.

words.definition: Fearless, bold, and ready to face danger without hesitation.
words.example: The intrepid explorer trekked alone across the frozen wilderness.
words.mnemonic: 'In-' (not) + 'trepid' (from trepidation, trembling) — not trembling, unafraid.

words.definition: Fearless and unwilling to be discouraged by danger or difficulty.
words.example: The dauntless firefighter charged into the blaze to reach the trapped child.
words.mnemonic: 'Daunt' (to intimidate) + '-less' — cannot be daunted; nothing frightens them off.

words.definition: Boldly daring and willing to take startling risks without fear.
words.example: Her audacious plan to scale the cliff barehanded stunned the entire team.
words.mnemonic: From Latin 'audax' (bold); think of someone brazen enough to be 'loud' and daring.

words.definition: Impossible to defeat, subdue, or discourage no matter the odds.
words.example: Despite years of setbacks, her indomitable will carried the movement forward.
words.mnemonic: 'In-' (not) + 'domit' (from dominate/tame) — cannot be tamed or dominated.

words.definition: Refusing to give up; keeping a firm grip on a goal or belief.
words.example: Despite three rejections, the tenacious reporter kept knocking until she finally got her interview.
words.mnemonic: Sounds like 'ten-acious' — picture holding on with all TEN fingers and never letting go.

words.definition: Persisting tirelessly and stubbornly despite difficulty, delay, or resistance.
words.example: His dogged pursuit of the truth wore down every witness who tried to stall him.
words.mnemonic: Picture a DOG clamped onto a bone, refusing to let go no matter how you pull.

words.definition: Stubbornly clinging to a purpose or opinion, often to an annoying degree.
words.example: The pertinacious salesman phoned every single day for a month until I agreed to meet.
words.mnemonic: 'Pertain' + 'tenacious' — he tenaciously sticks to anything that pertains to his goal.

words.definition: Refusing to change one's mind or actions despite good reasons to do so.
words.example: The obstinate toddler folded his arms and would not put on his shoes no matter what.
words.mnemonic: Contains 'ob-STIN' — think of a stubborn STAIN that just won't wash out.

words.definition: Determined to do what one wants while ignoring advice or warnings.
words.example: The headstrong young captain sailed straight into the storm despite every sailor's protest.
words.mnemonic: A 'strong head' that charges ahead — like a bull ramming forward, refusing direction.

words.definition: Stubbornly resistant to authority, control, discipline, or treatment.
words.example: The refractory recruit ignored every order, and the sergeant quickly lost his patience.
words.mnemonic: 'Re-fract' — like light that refracts and deflects control instead of accepting it.

words.definition: Behaving unpredictably and resisting guidance, often turning from the proper path.
words.example: Their wayward son skipped school for weeks and ignored every rule his parents set.
words.mnemonic: Goes its own 'way' — wandering wherever it wants, straying off the right way.

words.definition: Changing one's loyalties, feelings, or interests often and without good reason.
words.example: The fickle fan cheered for whichever team happened to be winning that particular week.
words.mnemonic: Sounds like 'pickle' — you can never pick one, always switching your choice.

words.definition: Likely to change suddenly and unpredictably, often becoming dangerous or violent.
words.example: The negotiations turned volatile, and within minutes shouting had replaced any polite discussion.
words.mnemonic: Think 'vola-' (to fly) — like volatile fuel evaporating, ready to blow up any moment.

words.definition: Playfully odd or fanciful, guided by sudden and unpredictable ideas.
words.example: Her whimsical garden was full of teapot birdhouses and little doors that led nowhere.
words.mnemonic: 'Whim' sits right inside it — acting on a passing whim, full of quirky fancies.

words.definition: Easy to manage, teach, or control; readily obedient.
words.example: The docile pony let the nervous children lead it around the ring without any fuss.
words.mnemonic: 'Doc-' from Latin docere (to teach) — a pupil a doctor can easily instruct.

words.definition: Easy to guide, manage, control, or deal with.
words.example: Once fed, the toddler became tractable and happily followed us through the entire museum.
words.mnemonic: From Latin 'tract' (to pull/lead) — you can lead it easily, like a tractor hauls a load.

words.definition: Excessively eager to obey or please others, like a lowly slave.
words.example: The servile waiter bowed repeatedly and agreed with every word the rude guest uttered.
words.mnemonic: 'Serv-' as in servant or serve — behaving like a groveling servant.

words.definition: Using insincere flattery toward powerful people to win favor or advantage.
words.example: The sycophantic aide praised the CEO's every idea, plainly hoping for a quick promotion.
words.mnemonic: 'Sick-o-fant' — a 'sick' fan who fawns over the boss to a sickening degree.

words.definition: Showing polite respect by yielding to another's wishes or opinions.
words.example: The new intern was deferential to senior staff, always asking before making any decision.
words.mnemonic: From 'defer' — you defer to someone, yielding to them out of respect.

words.definition: Reserved, quiet, and modest in manner, especially in a shy or proper way.
words.example: She kept a demure silence, eyes downcast, while the others boasted about their prizes.
words.mnemonic: DEMURE sounds like 'the mute' — a shy, quiet person who stays hushed and modest.

words.definition: Showing great, exact attention to small details of behavior, procedure, or etiquette.
words.example: He was punctilious about citing every source and replying to each email within the hour.
words.mnemonic: PUNCTILIOUS hides 'punctual' — picture a punctual clerk fussing over every tiny point (Latin 'punctum' = point).

words.definition: Very careful to do things correctly, with strict honesty and thoroughness.
words.example: The auditor was scrupulous, checking each figure twice and refusing every offered gift.
words.mnemonic: A SCRUPLE is a tiny moral doubt; someone full of scruples weighs every action carefully.

words.definition: Overly concerned with tiny rules or with showing off learning in a tedious way.
words.example: His pedantic corrections of everyone's grammar dragged the meeting out for another hour.
words.mnemonic: A PED-ANT is a tiny ant that crawls over every minor rule and detail.

words.definition: Behaving in a proud, superior way while looking down on other people.
words.example: With a haughty toss of her head, she swept past the crowd without a word.
words.mnemonic: HAUGHTY comes from French 'haut' (high) — acting as if high above everyone else.

words.definition: Acting as though you are better than others, full of scornful pride.
words.example: The supercilious clerk barely glanced up, sneering at the customer's simple question.
words.mnemonic: From Latin 'supercilium' (eyebrow) — picture a raised eyebrow arched in contempt.

words.definition: Openly rude and disrespectful, especially toward those who deserve respect.
words.example: The insolent recruit rolled his eyes and talked back to the sergeant mid-drill.
words.mnemonic: INSOLENT ~ 'in-sole' — imagine stomping the sole of your shoe on someone in disrespect.

words.definition: Boldly rude in a shameless, cheeky way that shows no respect.
words.example: The impudent child stuck out her tongue at the headmaster and giggled.
words.mnemonic: IMPUDENT starts with IMP — a mischievous little imp who cheekily misbehaves.

words.definition: Rudely bold or forward, showing a lack of proper respect.
words.example: It was impertinent of the intern to question the CEO's competence on day one.
words.mnemonic: IM + PERTINENT = 'not pertinent' — butting in where you don't belong, rudely.

words.definition: Generous and forgiving, especially toward a defeated or weaker rival.
words.example: In victory he was magnanimous, praising his opponent and shaking every hand.
words.mnemonic: MAGN (great) + ANIM (soul) — a person of 'great soul,' big-hearted and forgiving.

words.definition: Kind, generous, and wanting to do good for other people.
words.example: The benevolent donor quietly funded scholarships for every student who needed one.
words.mnemonic: BENE (good) + VOL (wish) — one who 'wishes good' upon others.

words.definition: Gentle and harmless in nature; not causing harm or damage.
words.example: The doctor smiled and said the lump was benign, requiring no treatment at all.
words.mnemonic: BENIGN opens with BENE (good) — a good, gentle thing that won't hurt you.

words.definition: Merciful and mild; of weather, pleasantly calm and not harsh.
words.example: The judge was clement, sparing the first-time offender any time behind bars.
words.mnemonic: CLEMENT sounds like 'clementine' — a sweet, mild little orange; sweet and gentle.

words.definition: Not strict; willing to forgive faults or punish only gently.
words.example: Their lenient parents rarely set a bedtime or enforced any household rules.
words.mnemonic: LENIENT ~ 'lean' — a lenient rule lets you lean back and relax (Latin 'lenis' = soft).

words.definition: Too willing to let someone have whatever they want; overly permissive.
words.example: The indulgent grandfather bought the twins every toy they so much as pointed at.
words.mnemonic: INDULGENT ~ 'in + dulce (sweet)' — picture spoiling someone with endless sweets.

words.definition: Patient and willing to endure delay or provocation without reacting in anger.
words.example: Even as the toddler hurled food across the room, the forbearing nanny just smiled and tidied up.
words.mnemonic: Read it as 'for-bearing' — a bear that holds back and chooses not to strike.

words.definition: Showing careful, anxious concern for another person's comfort, health, or wellbeing.
words.example: The solicitous nurse kept adjusting my pillow and asking whether I needed more water.
words.mnemonic: Sounds like a 'solicitor' who solicits — constantly checking in on you, fussing over your every need.

words.definition: Acting to help others without expecting any reward or benefit for yourself.
words.example: Donating a kidney to a total stranger was a purely altruistic act.
words.mnemonic: 'Altruistic' hides 'altru' from Latin 'alter' (other) — you put the OTHER person first.

words.definition: Feeling and showing sympathy for those who are suffering, and wanting to ease it.
words.example: The compassionate judge reduced the sentence after hearing about the boy's tragic home life.
words.mnemonic: Break it as 'com' (with) + 'passion' (suffering) — you suffer WITH someone and feel for them.

words.definition: Emotionally hardened and unfeeling toward the pain or troubles of others.
words.example: It was callous of him to laugh while she described losing her home in the fire.
words.mnemonic: A 'callus' is hardened skin — a callous person has a hardened heart, numb to feeling.

words.definition: Willing to hurt others or do harm to get what you want, without pity.
words.example: The ruthless CEO fired half the staff by email the week before the holidays.
words.mnemonic: 'Ruth' is an old word for pity or compassion, so 'ruth-less' means without any pity.

words.definition: Impossible to calm, satisfy, or win over once set against something.
words.example: Her implacable rival rejected every apology and every olive branch offered.
words.mnemonic: 'Im-placate-able' — you simply cannot placate or soothe them.

words.definition: Impossible to stop, change, or persuade; advancing relentlessly.
words.example: The inexorable rise of the floodwaters forced the whole town to flee overnight.
words.mnemonic: 'In-ex-orable' — cannot be prayed away; Latin 'orare' means 'to pray'.

words.definition: Strongly wanting to hurt someone who has wronged you, driven by a desire for revenge.
words.example: After the breakup she turned vindictive, sharing his private texts with everyone at work.
words.mnemonic: Hear 'vindicate' and 'vendetta' inside it — a vindictive person nurses a vendetta.

words.definition: Deliberately mean, wanting to annoy or hurt someone out of petty ill will.
words.example: In a spiteful move, he keyed his neighbor's car just because their tree shaded his lawn.
words.mnemonic: 'Spite' + 'ful' — full of spite, like spitting little jabs of malice at someone.

words.definition: Wishing harm or evil upon other people.
words.example: A malevolent grin spread across his face as he quietly sabotaged the experiment.
words.mnemonic: 'Mal' (bad) + 'volent' (wishing, as in volition) — wishing bad things on you.

words.definition: Marked by bitter, sharp, and angry words or feelings.
words.example: Their acrimonious argument ended with both of them slamming doors and refusing to speak.
words.mnemonic: 'Acri' echoes 'acrid' — a sharp, bitter taste, here in biting words.

words.definition: Rude, clumsy, and lacking good manners or social sensitivity.
words.example: His boorish behavior at dinner — chewing loudly and interrupting everyone — embarrassed his hosts.
words.mnemonic: A 'boor' sounds like a 'boar' — picture a wild pig snorting rudely at the table.

words.definition: Awkward, unrefined, and lacking grace or polish in manner or speech.
words.example: It seemed uncouth to show up at the funeral in flip-flops and a stained tank top.
words.mnemonic: 'Un' + 'couth' — 'couth' once meant 'known/refined,' so uncouth is un-refined, uncultured.

words.definition: Emotionally distant and unfriendly, deliberately keeping apart from others.
words.example: The new student stayed aloof, eating alone and sidestepping every conversation.
words.mnemonic: 'A-loof' sounds like standing 'aloft' above everyone, looking down and keeping distance.

words.definition: Expressing emotion or enthusiasm in an unrestrained, gushing manner.
words.example: Her effusive thank-you note ran three pages and mentioned every guest by name.
words.mnemonic: From Latin 'effundere,' to pour out — an effusive person pours praise everywhere.

words.definition: Full of intense passion, devotion, or eager enthusiasm.
words.example: An ardent fan, he drove nine hours just to catch the opening song.
words.mnemonic: Latin 'ardere' means to burn — an ardent heart burns hot.

words.definition: Showing intense energy and commitment toward a cause or goal.
words.example: The zealous new recruit stayed late reorganizing files nobody had asked him to touch.
words.mnemonic: It contains 'zeal' and sounds like 'jealous' — fiercely guarding a cause.

words.definition: Marked by forceful, powerful intensity of feeling or conviction.
words.example: Her vehement objection silenced the room before the vote could even begin.
words.mnemonic: Think 'vehicle-ment' — a feeling that hits you like a speeding vehicle.

words.definition: Sincere, serious, and heartfelt in purpose or effort.
words.example: His earnest apology, delivered with a shaky voice, convinced everyone he truly regretted it.
words.mnemonic: You 'earn' respect by being earnest — serious and sincere.

words.definition: Direct and honest in speech, without evasion.
words.example: When asked if the plan would fail, she was forthright: 'Yes, badly.'
words.mnemonic: It goes 'forth, right' at you — straight and unhesitating.

words.definition: Innocently frank and trusting, without cunning or hidden motive.
words.example: Her ingenuous question about why adults lie left the negotiators momentarily speechless.
words.mnemonic: An 'ingénue' is an innocent young character — both share that pure naivety.

words.definition: Free of deceit, cunning, or hidden motives; sincerely open.
words.example: The puppy-like, guileless grin made it impossible to believe he'd stolen anything.
words.mnemonic: 'Guile' (trickery) + 'less' — literally without any trickery.

words.definition: Falsely sincere; concealing true motives behind a pretense of honesty.
words.example: It was disingenuous of him to feign surprise when he'd secretly planned the whole thing.
words.mnemonic: 'Dis-' (not) + ingenuous (innocent) — the opposite of genuinely innocent.

words.definition: Using cunning, underhanded methods to achieve a hidden aim.
words.example: Through a devious series of favors and threats, he maneuvered into the chairman's seat.
words.mnemonic: Latin 'de via' means off the road — a devious person takes crooked, winding paths.

words.definition: Deceitfully saying one thing while intending or doing another.
words.example: The duplicitous agent sold the same secrets to both governments at once.
words.mnemonic: Shares 'dupli-' with 'duplicate' — two faces, two contradictory stories.

words.definition: Done quietly and secretly to escape notice.
words.example: She cast a furtive glance at the exit, hoping no one would see her slip away.
words.mnemonic: From Latin 'fur' (thief) — moving like a thief, on the sly.

words.definition: Kept secret or done stealthily to avoid disapproval.
words.example: He took a surreptitious photo of the exam, hiding his phone beneath the desk.
words.mnemonic: Think 'secret + reptile' — the act slithers past unseen.

words.definition: Clever at using tricks or schemes to gain an advantage.
words.example: The wily old fox doubled back through the stream and lost the hounds completely.
words.mnemonic: Someone wily is full of 'wiles' — cunning tricks up the sleeve.

words.definition: Showing sharp, practical judgment and clever awareness.
words.example: One shrewd investment early on funded the rest of her comfortable retirement.
words.mnemonic: Sounds like 'screwed' — cross a shrewd dealer and you'll be screwed.
